title: The gold of Santa Maria in Trastevere glitters as you walk: its tiles were set at angles
body: The apse mosaic of Santa Maria in Trastevere, in Rome, was made for Pope Innocent II, who rebuilt the church from 1140: he stands at the far left holding its model, beside Christ and Mary enthroned on a [background of gold](https://medievalmosaics.com/mosaics/118). Every piece of that gold is glass: a gold leaf less than half a micrometre thick, laid on a glass base and sealed under a thin glass cover, so a square metre of gold background holds under 10 grams of gold. The mosaicists pressed the pieces, called tesserae, one by one into wet mortar, and set the gold ones at [slightly different angles](https://flore.unifi.it/retrieve/083b1696-9046-409a-b5ea-9e1d5c9f9389/GuerraNeriRadtke_EurPhysJPlus_2023.pdf) to make the most of their shine. A flat mirror sends sunlight back one way only, so you would catch its glare from one spot; tiles tipped a few degrees each way send it in many directions, so some flash at you from almost anywhere, and different ones as you walk or as the Sun moves. Below the apse, the artist Pietro Cavallini added mosaics of the life of Mary in 1291.

slides.question: A square metre of the apse’s gold background is covered in gold glass tiles. How much gold does it hold, at most?
slides.explanation: Under 10 g. The gold in each tile is a leaf less than half a micrometre thick, and gold weighs 19.3 g per cubic centimetre.

slides.alt: Animation in lapis blue and gold: the apse of Santa Maria in Trastevere with Christ and Mary enthroned, a loupe on its tesserae, tiles pressed into wet mortar, a gold tessera taken apart, and sunlight traced off flat and tilted tiles to a viewer walking down the nave.

slides.prompt: Tilt the gold tiles and walk down the nave. Find a tilt that lets you catch a flash of sunlight from over two-thirds of the nave.
slides.takeaway: Flat, the gold flashes only from about 12 to 15 m away. Tipped up to about 8° either way, some tile flashes at you almost anywhere, and different ones as you walk: the gold glitters.

slides.alt: Photograph of the apse mosaic of Santa Maria in Trastevere: Mary, crowned, and Christ, with his arm around her, sit on one throne against a glittering gold background, between saints in white and blue robes; below them a band of Latin inscription and a frieze of white sheep on blue.
slides.caption: Christ and Mary enthroned in the apse of Santa Maria in Trastevere, between saints, with the Lamb of God and the sheep below.

slides.heading: How a gold tessera is made and set

steps.label: Beat gold into a leaf under 0.5 µm thick
Lay the leaf on a glass base
Seal it under a thin glass cover
Press it into wet mortar, slightly tilted

left.label: All tiles flat
left.text: Like one big mirror: sunlight bounces back in one direction, so you catch the glare from one spot only.

right.label: Tiles at varied angles
right.text: Each tile sends the light its own way, so some flash at you from almost anywhere, and others as you move.

slides.question: A mirror reflects light at the angle it is hit. Tip one gold tile by 2 degrees: how far does its reflection swing?
slides.explanation: Twice the tilt. Tipping the tile changes the angle the light comes in at by 2°, and the angle it leaves at by 2° more.

source.label: Guerra, Neri & Radtke (2023): Gold leaf tesserae, Eur. Phys. J. Plus
